newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Weather key to Australia anthrax outbreak.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Weather key to Australia anthrax outbreak.

text.p: Australia's A$2 billion a year dairy product export industry was waiting on Wednesday to see whether the spread of anthrax disease in cattle in the state of Victoria had been contained by a major vaccination programme.
Steve Tate, senior veterinary officer of Victoria's Department of Natural Resources and Energy, told Reuters that after a heavy vaccination effort much depended on the weather.
Hot and humid conditions after heavy rain encouraged spread of anthrax, Tate said. Weather in the affected areas was presently sunny and pleasant with cool nights, he said.
"We're hopeful its under control," he said.
Most cattle in the high-risk area have now been vaccinated.
Cattle deaths in the vaccinated area had ceased and fewer new cases of infection were being reported now, Tate said.

A total of 9,000 cattle had been vaccinated as of Wednesday morning, a rise of 1,000 on the day before, Peter McLaughlin, a spokesman for the Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, told Reuters. He said that as of Wednesday morning, 94 properties had been vaccinated, 29 more than on Tuesday.
The number of confirmed properties affected stood at 31, up one on the day before, while confirmed cattle deaths on Wednesday morning stood at 68, two more than Tuesday, he said.

One worker who handled cattle carcasses has been infected and was undergoing penicillin treatment in hospital, Dr Rosemary Lester of the Department of Human Services public health division's infectious diseases unit said in a statement.
The knackery where the worker was infected had been closed and disinfected as soon as the outbreak was realised.
All infected cattle were now being burnt and buried on the infected properties, which were under quarantine, she said.

"Anthrax is a disease of animals which rarely affects humans. There has never been a case of anthrax reported from persons drinking milk from infected cows, but, as a precaution, milk is held for eight hours after milking to see if the animal develops anthrax," Lester said.
David Loutit, chief executive officer of the Victorian Dairy Industry Authority, expects a "fairly minor" impact on exports.
"Obviously it's a serious matter (but) from everything we hear people (know) the matter is under control and the product is safe," he said.

Malcolm Elder, spokesman for the Department of Human Services, said anthrax infection was not contained in pasteurised milk, which was held for the eight hours, while the heat drying of processed foods also killed any infection.

Australia is forecast to export A$1.8 billion worth of dairy products in 1996/97 (July-June), with Europe a traditional market but with strongest growth in Asia, where the biggest customer is Japan. Rejection by Japanese importers of Australian dairy products would create a "virtually immediate" effect, although none had been felt so far, an official with a leading Japanese trading house told Reuters on Wednesday.
The anthrax-affected area supplies about 30 percent of Australia's dairy products, while Victoria produces about 50 percent of the Australian total.
Milk powders form 70 percent-80 percent of Australia's dairy exports to Japan, worth almost A$310.0 million in 1995/96.
Australia's other main dairy product markets in Asia are the Philippines, which took almost A$240.0 million in 1995/96, Malaysia, which took A$150.0 million, and Thailand, which took A$147.0 million.
Anthrax, a bacterial infection, causes rapid death in cattle, sheep and goats which eat contaminated material.
